claims.statement: Four scanners — Semgrep (TS/JS + Python source), cargo audit (Rust deps), pnpm audit (JS deps) and pip-audit (Python deps) — feed one normalized findings report and one blocking `sast` CI job; the tier is disjoint from DAST (which exercises the running app) and from infra-image scanning (which scans pulled third-party images rather than first-party code or dependency graphs).

pip-audit audits the INSTALLED venv rather than a requirements file, and covers four Python surfaces (`agents/movie-assistant` plus the three `mcp-servers/*`), each with its own dependency graph and runtime classification; an unsynced surface fails the whole scan instead of being silently skipped, and CI syncs all four venvs.

pip-audit findings are project-qualified (`mcp-servers/web-api-mcp:click@8.5.0`), so allowlist `locationPattern`s should normally be anchored to one surface; two static, finding-independent checks enforce this at scan time — `assertKnownPythonSurfaces` fails the scan for a Python project on disk that is not registered in `PYTHON_SURFACES`, and `assertPipAuditAllowlistShape` fails an anchored pattern naming a surface that does not exist (an unanchored pattern stays legal as a deliberate cross-surface suppression).

The tier is keyless and fail-closed: all advisory data (Semgrep registry, RustSec DB, npm advisories, OSV) is fetched anonymously at scan time, and any fetch failure fails that scanner — recorded in `scanners[].error` with a non-zero exit — rather than reporting a false clean; no secret is ever required.

The SCA half runs full on every push unconditionally and is never path-gated, because a newly published advisory can hit an unchanged dependency; consequently `main` can legitimately go red on a dependency nobody touched, and this recurs.

A finding blocks the gate only when it is High/Critical AND either SAST or runtime-scope SCA; dependency scope is derived per ecosystem across the whole workspace, so hand-checking scope requires a recursive query — `pnpm why <pkg> --prod` WITHOUT `-r` runs at the repo root only, prints nothing for a dep runtime-reachable via a sub-package, and that empty output is the wrong scope rather than 'dev-only' (this mistake wrongly accused the gate of a bug on 2026-07-21).
A fixable High must be bumped rather than allowlisted — the allowlist is for findings with no fix yet — and suppression is gate-only, so an allowlisted finding stays visible in the reports.

`p/secrets` is deliberately absent from the Semgrep config set because `secret-scan.mjs` remains the sole owner of credential detection; enabling it here would double-gate and split the allowlist across two owners.

Rust source is out of Semgrep's scope: clippy covers Rust source patterns and cargo-audit covers only Rust dependencies, so the mc-service Rust surface relies on clippy plus review for the patterns Semgrep enforces elsewhere (the no-JWT-payload-tracing rule therefore covers TS/JS and Python only).

Semgrep resolves its community `p/*` packs from its public registry at scan time, so an unreachable registry fails the scanner closed and leaves `findings.json` empty while the gate still exits 0 — a green that proves nothing; adding the host to `.devcontainer/egress-allowlist.json` is only HALF the change because egress is enforced in two layers and the host-side sandbox policy is scoped per sandbox and does not re-read the committed file, so a Semgrep result must be sanity-checked (probe the host, or run `--only semgrep`) before it is trusted.

When Semgrep cannot run, 'the tier cannot run here' is the wrong conclusion: only Semgrep needs the registry host, so `--only pnpm-audit` (or cargo-audit / pip-audit) produces a real, complete SCA report locally, which matters because every dependency-floor remediation is an SCA finding; the corollary is to check the finding COUNT rather than the exit code, since a 0-finding report and a report with no blocking findings print the same green.

Each keyed entry in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `overrides:` map is a range keyed on a range, so both halves must move together; `scripts/check-override-consistency.mjs` enforces key's exclusive upper bound == value's inclusive lower bound on every pull request, scoped to keys carrying an `@<range>` suffix (plain pins such as `react-dom` and `postcss` are out of scope, and an unparseable half is refused out loud with exit 2 rather than skipped).

Unmatched allowlist entries are reported under `UNMATCHED ENTRIES` but never block; an entry keyed on an exact advisory id does not expire when a scanner switches identifier namespace (the measured pip-audit CVE → PYSEC case), it just quietly stops suppressing — and unmatched detection is deliberately evaluated only for scanners that produced at least one finding, so a skipped, failed or clean scanner never flags its whole entry set.

Expiry has an inclusive 14-day warning window before an entry stops suppressing: `EXPIRING SOON` reports it while it still suppresses and without moving the exit code, `EXPIRED` re-blocks and explains which entry and which `addedBy` covered it; the window length is defined once as `WARNING_WINDOW_DAYS` in `scripts/allowlist-expiry.mjs` and imported by both gates, and the dedicated `--check-expiring` mode runs weekly (Friday) in the `infra-image-scan` workflow, never on a pull request.

The weekly `--check-expiring` run cannot flag an unmatched SAST entry because that job produces no SAST report, so unmatched detection is skipped there and the CVE→PYSEC class of silent non-suppression is visible only in the report-only output of a normal gate run; the report-absent path must announce the missing report rather than assume a clean pass (a report that exists but will not parse is still exit 2), and it must not throw — when it did, the step aborted and `bash -e` skipped the infra-image expiry check on the next line, leaving BOTH expiry tiers dead from 2026-09-12 until the 2026-09-25 weekly sweep exposed it.

Remediation, not re-dating, is the rule for an accepted finding: deleting or extending an `expiry` is how a time-box becomes permanent, and a time-boxed acceptance can be discharged by a route its own justification did not anticipate — the `image-size` entries were cleared because the dependency left the tree entirely (metro dropped it), not by the fix version the entry predicted.

Since feature 058 the gate prints an `OVERRIDE LEVERS` section naming which lever clears a finding whose package already carries an override — `refresh-lockfile` when the range already permits the published fix, `raise-floor` (with both halves of the suggested override) when it does not; this distinction cost ten days of red once because `fast-uri`'s override already permitted the fix while the lockfile pinned the vulnerable version, and `nanoid` repeated it eight days later. The advice is computed per resolution rather than per package, is advisory only and never changes the exit code, and prints for non-blocking findings too so a cheap fix can be made before severity promotes it.

Renovate's `lockFileMaintenance` now clears most lockfile-pinned findings weekly, but its `schedule` key in `renovate.json` carries its own default (`before 4am on monday`) that beats the inherited top-level value and intersects neither cron under either DST offset, so deleting it as redundant silently disables the refresh; these refresh PRs also run `app-e2e` because a bad transitive floor is a build-time break that `nx test` passes over.

Allowlist `locationPattern`s are matched against paths normalized to forward slashes so one pattern is portable across the Windows dev host and the Linux CI runner; a backslash pattern matches nothing on the runner yet passes silently on the Windows side, so the finding re-blocks in CI.

A Semgrep rule it could not RUN is reported in the native output's `errors[]`, never in `results[]`, so a blinded rule contributes zero findings and is indistinguishable from a remediated one — its allowlist entry lands in `UNMATCHED ENTRIES` reading as 'remediated already'. Measured on `main` 2026-09-06, `gha-curl-pipe-shell` re-parses a step's `run:` block as Bash, cannot read the ci-log-step heredoc wrapping nearly every run-step, and produced 36 errors and 0 findings while six `curl … | sh` lines sat in the workflows. The gate now names this itself via `RULES THAT COULD NOT RUN` and annotates the `UNMATCHED` entry it explains, both advisory and never moving the exit code; coverage for the pattern is restored by the text-level custom rule `mcm-ci-curl-pipe-shell`, whose accepted installer URLs live in the rule rather than the allowlist.

Attributing Semgrep errors to a rule requires reading the error message, not only the structured field: the pinned Semgrep populates `rule_id` on an `Internal matching error` but not on a `PartialParsing` one, where the rule name appears only in the prose — keying on the field alone attributed 3 of that run's 36 errors, understating the blindness by an order of magnitude.

On a pull request `--scope changed` builds an explicit target list, so the extension filter in `isScanTarget()` — not the rule's own `paths:` — decides what a PR is gated on; workflow YAML was absent from that list until item #224, meaning a `curl … | sh` added to a workflow was gated on nothing and first appeared on the post-merge full scan.

The same PR-vs-push gap opened a second time through Dockerfiles, which have no extension: PR #422 added a Dockerfile whose `guardrails / sast` passed, and the post-merge full scan then failed on `dockerfile.security.missing-user-entrypoint`; Dockerfiles are now in the filter (item #426) and the whole surface was enumerated once rather than reactively.

That enumeration is now standing rather than a snapshot: on a full-scope report, a blocking SAST finding whose file `isScanTarget()` rejects fails the gate with its own section and exit path, `GATE-SCOPE ASYMMETRY`. Three properties make the guard real — it counts suppressed findings as well as failures (the minio Dockerfile case was allowlisted, so the gate was green and the asymmetry invisible); it excludes SCA (audits ignore `--scope` entirely) and changed-scope reports (every file there was by definition a target); and a report with no usable `generatedAtScope` is a hard error, because a missing field must not be able to switch off the guard the way a missing file class switched off the thing it guards. The remedy it names is widening the changed-scope filter, not adding an allowlist entry.

`node scripts/sast-scan.mjs --test-rules` proves the custom rules before a scan is trusted: it runs `semgrep --test` over `security/sast/rules/` and additionally fails if any rule lacks a fixture, because `semgrep --test` SKIPS an unfixtured rule and still prints `N/N ✓` (measured `4/4 ✓ All tests passed` with five rule files present). The Semgrep pin lives only in `sast-scan.mjs` — the CI step carries no second copy to drift — and the step runs ahead of the scan on the same prove-the-instrument-then-use-it reasoning as the gate selftest.

A red `sast` gate whose output says `TRANSPORT/SERVICE ERROR` is a third-party outage that survived the bounded retry and should be re-run, not a security finding: three scanners reach a third party on the required gate's critical path (pip-audit → osv.dev, cargo-audit → the RustSec advisory DB, pnpm audit → the npm registry), and measured 2026-09-13 on run 3328 the gate went red on a pip-audit `ServiceError` from osv.dev while the scan had otherwise completed clean (`findings=16 blocking=0`). Since item #449 such failures are retried 3 times with exponential backoff (2 s, 4 s) before a verdict, the job log naming the attempt, and the failure output states explicitly that it is NOT a security finding.

The retry preserves two properties that must not be simplified away: fail-closed (exhausting the attempts still throws, so a scanner that could not run never reports clean) and a deliberately narrow classification (anything unrecognised is treated as real and fails on the first attempt, so a genuine fault — an unsynced venv, an unparseable lockfile, a panic — is not delayed by the whole backoff budget). `scripts/__tests__/sast-scan-retry.guard.test.mjs` pins both directions plus the word 'error' alone not being a signature.

The classifier and retry driver live in `scripts/lib/scanner-retry.mjs`, shared with `infra-image-scan.mjs` since item #495 (Trivy's vulnerability-DB fetch needed the same behaviour) because the hard part is the signature list and a signature learned from one scanner's outage is what the other needs next. Its HTTP-status signatures require the status CODE rather than the bare phrase: `Service Unavailable` / `Bad Gateway` / `Too Many Requests` also occur in advisory TITLES, as does `Read timed out`, and since the classifier is handed `stderr + stdout` on the cargo-audit and pip-audit paths, a bare phrase would have retried a real finding three times and then reported it anyway.

This page is a derived summary of the SAST/SCA operator runbook, which owns the full scanner matrix, local invocation, CI step list and the step-by-step red-gate playbook; `security/sast/README.md` owns the allowlist field rules and full expiry semantics. The page repairs its broken anchor to the egress-allowlist section by pointing at the document that owns it, `docs/runbooks/devcontainer-sandbox.md#4-egress-allowlist`.
